The street grid was thus applied in San Jose; in fact, the grid is the basis for land division in all seven of the proposed project areas.
The second seminal event with respect to San Jose's development (and for the rest of the industrial world as well) was the mass-production of the automobile. To emphasize the point, one writer described the man driving an automobile as ". . . a different kind of man to the horse-and-buggy men who had ruled the world since Alexander the Great." The automobile changed the world qualitatively; perception was different at sixty miles an hour than at ten. The time from its mass introduction in the 1920's to the present 1970's has been spent reworking urban scale, form, architecture to fit the new motive. Intermediate local solutions include the difference between West San Carlos Street and Stevens Creek Boulevard; Bayshore Highway (1937) V. Highway 280; and with respect to residential development, Almaden Valley vs. Northside, for example. To at least some extent, all seven of the project areas discussed below reflect some influence made by the automobile.
Alma CNRA:
The Alma area possesses several of the attributes of the previously-discussed areas. On the north and east Alma is bounded by auto-oriented commercial strips. To the south, the Western Pacific Railroad has fostered industrial activity. To the west, Almaden Expressway breaks up the area's street grid, thus giving the area a fourth logical boundary. The regular lots of the grid contain houses of approximately the same age and style, as in Olinder or Northside.
Yet, despite these similarities, Alma does not "feel" like the other comparable neighborhoods. And to the eye the condition of the housing is quite frequently deteriorated. Also, only rarely does any street landscaping occur.
The condition of this neighborhood raises several questions which lack adequate answers. There are very few clues in Alma's built environment which explain the relatively poor condition of that environment (with respect to the other project areas), or the inhospitable feeling which the neighborhood gives off.
Alviso CNRA:
Like five of the other six project areas, north of Grand Boulevard, Alviso is laid out on a grid pattern, with blocks about three times as long as wide. The blocks are subdivided into regular lots. Built upon the lots are houses generally constructed between 1920-1940, with perhaps some older residences mixed in. The pattern is straightforward; the condition of the houses appears usually fair. There is little street landscaping, although frequently the lots are bordered by a low fence, which visually serves to separate the territories of street and lot.
